newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Nomura rates Slovak VSZ shares as a buy.
newsitem.headline: Nomura rates Slovak VSZ shares as a buy.

text.p: Shares of VSZ a.s., Slovakia's main steel producer, are rated a buy, an equity report by Nomura Research Institute said.

The report based its recommendation on a January 21 price of 640 crowns per share. The stock closed at 650 crowns on Friday and market analysts said strong demand was expected to push the price further up in the near future.
"We do not put an upper limit on our recommendations. We recommend shares as such," Nomura's Sean Murphy told Reuters.
The share price represents 34 percent of net asset value, estimated by Nomura at 1,887 crowns for 1996.

The report said 1996 saw the first positive marketing results when increased penetration into EU markets and a modest recovery in eastern European steel demand shielded the firm from most of the effects of a western European steel slump.
"Though profits will fall in 1996, this is measured against an exceptional peak in the steel cycle in 1995 and the decline should not be as much as that of western competitors," it said.
It added that compared with western steel firms, VSZ appears extremely profitable and that return on capital employed and return on equity are more than twice as high as western European averages.

Nomura forecast VSZ consolidated pre-tax profit to fall to around 4.5 billion crowns in 1996, from 6.3 billion in the previous year. Pre-tax profit for 1997 and 1998 are expected to total 4.7 billion crowns and 4.65 billion, respectively.

"Declining tax rates should allow 1996 earnings per share to reach 124.6 crowns, down 20 percent against EPS of 155 crowns in 1995." EPS is forecast at 139.9 and 149 crowns for 1997 and 1998 respectively.
The company has only made available preliminary unconsolidated after-tax profit at its main steel production unit, VSZ Ocel, totalling around 1.3 billion crowns, up some 100 million crowns from 1995.
However the report did express concern over the results of VSZ's extensive diversification strategy.
"The (strategy) is a definite worry. Investments ranging from football clubs to banks do not seem the hallmark of a focused steel maker," Nomura said.

It said it considered the financing of such purchases and their effectiveness as significant issues, and noted that there was an absence of communication about this matter between the company and its shareholders.
